title: The created body of Christ shown by his passion and resurrection
english: If anyone says that the body of Christ is uncreated, and does not confess that the uncreated God the Word himself displayed his incarnation from created humanity and became man as it is written, let him be anathema. For how can a body be called uncreated? What is uncreated is also incapable of suffering, and can be neither wounded nor touched. But Christ, rising from the dead, showed the disciples the marks of the nails and the wound made by the lance, and his body able to be touched, and he entered through closed doors. He did this to display both the works of his divinity and the reality of his body: although he was otherwise God, he was recognized as man; and although he was truly man, God was nevertheless demonstrated from his own works.

Explication: uncreated = impassible/intangible vs risen body handled behind shut doors

title: The flesh is not consubstantial with the divinity
english: If anyone says that the flesh of Christ is consubstantial with the divinity, and does not confess that he himself was in the form of God and was God before the ages, and that he emptied himself and took the form of a servant, as it is written, let him be anathema. For how can flesh that came into being in time be called consubstantial with the sempiternal divinity? What is consubstantial is what is the same in nature and in sempiternity, without change.

title: Christ became man by incarnation, not by assuming a pre-existing perfect man
english: If anyone says that Christ assumed a perfect man, as one from the prophets, and does not confess that the Lord himself was made man by incarnation from the Virgin, born in Bethlehem, raised in Nazareth, and who showed his progress in age and fulfilled the course of time; was baptized in the Jordan, and received this testimony from the Father: "This is my beloved Son," as it is written; let him be anathema. For how can it be said that a perfect man was assumed by the Lord, as one from the prophets, when the Lord himself was made man by incarnation from the Virgin? Therefore it is written: "The first man from the earth, earthly" (1 Corinthians 15:47). After the one who was formed from the earth went to the earth, the second man, who was made, ascended into the heavens. And Scripture speaks of a first Adam and a last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45). And just as it is acknowledged that the second is from the first, as regards the flesh; from which he is both man, and the Son of Man, Christ: so it is also testified that the second is the Savior of the first, for whose sake he also descended from heaven. Since the Word, descending from heaven, and made man, ascended into the heavens; therefore he is also said to be the second Adam from heaven.

title: The virgin birth and conception by the Holy Spirit
english: If anyone says that Christ was born from the seed of a man from the Virgin, just as all other human beings are born, and does not confess that he was incarnate by the Holy Spirit and from the holy Virgin Mary, and made a human being from the seed of David, as it is written, let him be anathema. How can Christ be said to have been born from the seed of a man from the Virgin, when the holy Gospel and the Angel himself testify that the Virgin Mary said: "How will this be to me, since I do not know a man?" That is why the one who announced the news to Mary said: "The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who is born from you will be called the Son of the Most High." And he says to Joseph: "Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife. For what is born in her is from the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and they will call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins."

title: One Son Before Ages and in Last Times
english: If anyone says that one is the Son of God before the ages, and another the one who appeared in the last times, and does not confess that the same one is he before the ages and who appeared in the last times, as it is written, let him be anathema. How can it be said that one is the Son of God before the ages, and another in the last times, when the Lord himself says, "Before Abraham came to be, I am"? And, "Because I went forth from the Father, and I come; and again I go to my Father" (John 8:58; John 16:28).

title: The same Word suffered in his own flesh
english: If anyone says that the one who suffered is one person, and the one who did not suffer is another, and does not confess that the same Word of God, incapable of suffering and unchangeable, suffered without change in his own flesh, as it is written, let him be anathema.

How can it be said that the one who suffered is one, and the one who did not suffer is another? The Lord himself says, "The son of man must suffer many things and be killed, and rise again on the third day" (Luke 9:22). He also says, "When you see the son of man sitting at the right hand of the Father." And, "When the son of man comes in the glory of his Father" (Mark 8:38).

title: Against Dividing Christ into Two Separate Persons
english: If anyone says that Christ is a perfect human being separately, and the Word of God separately, and does not confess one Lord Jesus Christ, just as it is written, let him be anathema. How can anyone say that Christ is a perfect human being separately, and the Word of God separately, when the Lord himself says: "Why do you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth that I heard from the Father?" For he did not give a mere human being for us, but the Word of God made human for us handed over himself for us. That is why he says: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." But he was speaking about the temple of his body (John 8:40; John 2:19-21).

title: Christ Unchangeable in Spirit Yet Corruptible in Flesh
english: If anyone says that Christ is changeable or alterable, and does not confess him unchangeable in spirit and corruptible in flesh, let him be anathema. By what reason can anyone say that Christ is changeable or variable? For the Lord himself says: “I am, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6). And again: “His soul was not left in hell, nor did his flesh see corruption” (Acts 2:31).

title: Christ's body and soul are complete, and his sufferings are real human passions
english: If anyone says that the body of Christ is inanimate or without a mind, and does not confess that he is a perfect human being in every respect, one and the same, let him be anathema.

How could anyone say that the body of Christ is without a soul or without a mind? Disturbance, pain, and fear belong neither to inanimate flesh nor to a mindless soul; nor do they belong to the unchanging divinity; nor are they a display of an empty appearance; nor are they a defect of giving way in human weakness. Rather, the Word was showing in himself the sufferings of our nature, taking up a portion given for suffering. As it is written: "For he himself has taken up our infirmities and borne our sicknesses." Disturbance, pain, and fear are sicknesses of the soul; exhaustion, sleep, and wounding are infirmities of the flesh.
notes_covered: Cap. XI anathema against a body of Christ without soul or mind

title: Anathema against docetism; Christ's real life, passion, and victory through flesh; doxology; call to simple faith and conduct; mystery of the incarnation; warning against word-strife
english: Let anyone who says that Christ appeared in the world only in opinion and fictitiously, and who does not confess that he came in the flesh, be anathema. How can anyone claim that Christ appeared supposedly and fictitiously to the world — Christ, I say, born in Bethlehem, brought to the circumcision of the flesh, carried by Simeon, raised by his parents up to his twelfth year, and obedient to them; baptized in the Jordan, nailed to the cross, and raised from the dead? Therefore, when it is said: He was troubled in spirit, he was saddened in soul, he was wounded in body, these are the names of the passions according to the constitution of our nature, so as to show that he was born a man in the world, and lived among men in our likeness, yet without sin. For he was born in Bethlehem according to the flesh, as was fitting for God, with the heavenly angels recognizing their Lord, and praising God wrapped in swaddling clothes in a manger, and saying: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will (Luke 2:14). He was nurtured in Nazareth. Sitting in the midst of the Teachers, he showed himself to be God, and moved them to wonder at his wisdom beyond the time of his age, according to the flesh, as the Gospel account narrates. He was baptized in the Jordan, not to receive sanctification for himself, but so that he might dispense to others a share in sanctification. He was tempted in the wilderness, yet not overcome by the temptation, but set our temptations against the tempter’s provocation, so as to show the tempter to be empty. Therefore he says: Take courage, I have conquered the world (John 16:33). He did not oppose a divine struggle, but displayed his own flesh victorious over passion, and death, and corruption: so that through the very flesh by which sin entered the world, and through sin death reigned in all people (Romans 5:12), through the same flesh according to likeness, sin might be condemned in the flesh (Romans 8:3); and the ruler of sin who tempts might be conquered; and death might be dissolved, so that it would not reign; and corruption might vanish in the burial of the body; and the firstfruits of the resurrection might be shown (1 Corinthians 15:20), and the beginning of justice in the world might be exercised through faith; and the kingdom of heaven might be announced to people, and communion of God with people might be entered. For this grace let us glorify the Father, who gave his only-begotten Son for the life of the world; let us glorify the Holy Spirit, who works in us and gives us life, and grants gifts for entering into communion with God; and let us not search out the Gospel teaching curiously with dry words, carrying around endless questions and battles of words, and making a plain and easy and right discourse about faith rough; but rather let us work the work of faith, love peace, prefer concord, keep unity and joining together, cultivate love, by which God is placated. Just as it is not ours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power (Acts 1:7); yet we must believe that there will be an end of this age, and a future manifestation of the coming age, and a revelation of judgment, and the coming of the Son of God (Acts 1:11), and the repayment of works (2 Corinthians 5:10), and the possession of the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 25:34): so it is not ours to know how the Son of God became man. For this is a great mystery, just as it is written: Who shall narrate his generation? because his life is taken from the earth (Isaiah 53:8). But we must believe that the Son of God became man according to the Scriptures; and that he was seen on earth, and lived among men, as the Scriptures teach, in our likeness, without sin; and that he died for us, and rose from the dead, as it is written; and that he was taken up into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father, from where he will come to judge the living and the dead, as Scripture teaches: lest perhaps while we contend with words among ourselves, some may blaspheme the doctrine of faith; and what is said may happen: Because of you my name is always blasphemed among the nations (Isaiah 52:5; Romans 2:24; Ezekiel 36:20-23).

Interminatas quaestiones follows 1 Timothy 1:4 (genealogiis interminatis, quae quaestiones praestant); at circunferentes a marginal gloss is too blurred to read.
Placatur rendered “is appeased” (made favourable).
The second “in our likeness, without sin” is not cited again (Hebrews 4:15 given above).
At in caelos assumptus sit the margin has al. ascendit; text kept, cited to Mark 16:19 (assumptus est in caelum, et sedet a dextris Dei).
“Judge the living and the dead” also stands in Acts 10:42 and 1 Peter 4:5.

The last quotation follows Isaiah 52:5 in its LXX form (“because of you … continually … among the Gentiles”), which Romans 2:24 also quotes; at nomen meum the margin has al. nomen Dei (partly obscured), which is the form of Romans 2:24; text kept.
The editor's margin sigla on pp. 6–8 were read only at scan resolution; each citation here was checked from the wording.
source_ref: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia, Duodecim Capita de Fide, Cap. XII (anathema + interpretatio), printed pp. 6-8 (PDF pp. 30-32)
orientation: Gregory closes the treatise by anathematizing anyone who says Christ only seemed to appear, then recounts the concrete events of Christ's life to prove his real humanity, explains how his flesh wins victory over sin and death, offers a trinitarian doxology, urges believers to pursue faith's works rather than curious word-battles, affirms the mystery of the incarnation, and warns that disputing over words blasphemes the faith.
